chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub informed us, from Muhammad ibn Yahya and Ahmad ibn Idris, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from as-Siyari, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from his brother al-Husayn, from his father Ali ibn Yaqteen, who said:
Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far said to me: "O Ali, the Shia have been brought up with hopes since two hundred years."

Yaqteen said to his son Ali ibn Yaqteen: "What is the matter? What was said to us occurred, but what was said to you did not occur?" (He meant the matter of the Banu al-Abbas). Ali said to him: "What was said to you and what was said to us came from the same source, except that the time of your matter arrived, so you were given its pure fulfillment and it happened as it was said to you. But the time of our matter had not yet arrived, so we justified it with hopes. If it had been said to us that this matter would not occur until two hundred or three hundred years, our hearts would harden and most people would revert from faith to Islam. But they said to us: 'How swift it is and how near,' to win over the hearts of people and to bring the deliverance closer."

key_terms.الْأَمَانِي: Hopes or expectations used as a theological justification for delay
key_terms.مِنْ مَخْرَجٍ وَاحِدٍ: From the same source or origin

ai.seo_question: Why did the Shia wait for the Imam for centuries without a fixed date?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Nu'mani’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* elucidates the doctrine of *al-amani* (expectations/hopes) as a strategic divine measure to sustain communal faith during the prolonged occultation of the Mahdi. Ali ibn Yaqteen explains that while the Abbasid rise occurred promptly, the Imamate's delay was veiled in indefinite hope to prevent spiritual fatigue and mass apostasy, illustrating the Shia concept of *hikma* (wisdom) in divine timing.
